title: Randomized evasiveness conjecture
formal: Is there an absolute constant \(c>0\) and an integer \(n_0\ge 2\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_0\) and every nonconstant monotone graph property \(P\) on n vertices, its randomized adjacency-query complexity with two-sided error at most \(1/3\) satisfies \(R_{1/3}(P)\ge c n^2\)? Both c and \(n_0\) must be independent of P. This card asks for the bounded-error randomized evasiveness conjecture.
why: This conjecture asks whether monotonicity and invariance under vertex names force essentially complete inspection even when random errors are allowed. It is a broad structural lower-bound question covering many graph recognition tasks at once. Its resolution would sharply delimit the power of randomized access to an exact graph property and explain why proximity testing can behave so differently.
status_note: The bounded-error conjecture is explicit in the checked 2002 and 2020 sources and is restated as open in the Winter 2025 notes. Targeted later-work searches on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution. Original model definitions, not informal randomized-complexity labels, govern the reported lower bounds. The search is bounded and cited proofs were not independently verified.
review_note: Completed individual review against P versus NP on 2026-09-14; see research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

progress.text: Buhrman and de Wolf explicitly list the bounded-error randomized quadratic lower bound as Open Problem 6 and distinguish it from exact deterministic evasiveness.

Chakrabarti and Khot publish a universal \(\Omega(n^{4/3}(\log n)^{1/3})\) bound for zero-error randomized expected query cost. Its model is stated explicitly here because the informal term randomized complexity can otherwise hide the distinction.

Jain and Zhang extend an influence-based query lower bound to two-sided error and expected query cost. This provides bounds in a model allowing mistakes, without establishing the conjectured universal quadratic rate.
Grossman, Komargodski and Naor separately formulate the bounded-error conjecture in their work on instance complexity; it is not identified with their additional instance-optimality conjecture.
Aaronson, Ben-David, Kothari, Rao and Tal prove the optimal universal \(\Omega(n)\) quantum-query bound for nontrivial monotone graph properties. The theorem concerns quantum query complexity.
Blais’s Winter 2025 course notes continue to state the randomized evasiveness conjecture as open. These notes provide a dated status statement rather than a new lower-bound theorem.

importance.reason: A major longstanding structural conjecture in query complexity, asserting a universal quadratic barrier for randomized recognition across all nontrivial monotone graph properties.

sentences: A monotone graph property is invariant under vertex renaming and cannot be destroyed by adding edges.
The conjecture says every nonconstant such property needs a quadratic number of adjacency queries even with randomized error at most one third.
The query bound is worst-case over graphs and random choices, while the error guarantee holds separately for each graph.
Zero-error expected-cost lower bounds and the solved quantum analogue concern distinct computational models.
A resolution would establish or refute a universal information barrier for randomized exact graph recognition.

definitions: Let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and let \(E_n\) be the set of unordered pairs of distinct elements of \([n]\). An input \(x\in\{0,1\}^{E_n}\) describes a finite simple undirected graph: \(x_e=1\) means e is an edge. Every one of the \(2^{\binom n2}\) assignments is a valid input. A graph property is a function \(P:\{0,1\}^{E_n}\to\{0,1\}\) invariant under every permutation of the vertices, with the permutation acting on each edge’s two endpoints. Monotone means \(x_e\le y_e\) for every e implies \(P(x)\le P(y)\). Nonconstant means some input has value 0 and another has value 1; for monotone P the empty graph has value 0 and the complete graph value 1. No monotonicity across different vertex counts is imposed. A deterministic query tree is a finite binary tree whose internal nodes name edges, whose outgoing branches carry the possible queried bits, and whose leaves carry output bits. On input x it follows the branch specified by each queried \(x_e\). Its cost on x is the number of queries along that path. A randomized query algorithm is a probability distribution \(\mu\), independent of x, on such trees. It has cost at most q if every tree with positive probability has depth at most q. It computes P with error at most \(1/3\) when \(\Pr_{T\sim\mu}[T(x)=P(x)]\ge 2/3\) for every input x. Define \(R_{1/3}(P)\) as the smallest such integer q. The distribution and trees may depend on P and n. Sampling, storage and all computation on previously obtained answers are uncharged; only queries revealing one adjacency bit are counted. There is no uniformity or efficient-construction requirement on the trees, and no description of P is part of the queried graph. Queries may be adaptive. Input distributions, promises that a no-instance is far from P, quantum access, certificates and other graph oracles are absent. Cost is worst-case over both the graph and trees in the support, not expected over those choices. The only approximation allowed is the stated probability of an incorrect membership bit. In particular, a graph missing P by a single edge still requires the same success guarantee.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed universal lower-bound proposition. A positive answer requires one c and one \(n_0\) working for all the indicated graph properties and all \(n\ge n_0\). Its negation is: for every \(c>0\) and every integer \(N\ge 2\), there exist an integer \(n\ge N\) and a nonconstant monotone graph property P on n vertices with \(R_{1/3}(P)<c n^2\). A refutation must establish this quantified failure, not just a constant-factor saving from querying every edge. A result only for zero-error randomized algorithms, deterministic algorithms, selected properties, or proximity testing does not by itself settle the bounded-error target.

context_blocks.text: Connectedness is monotone: adding edges cannot disconnect a connected graph. It is also independent of how its vertices are named. The conjecture encompasses every property with these two formal features, including properties chosen separately at different graph sizes, rather than only a fixed list of familiar algorithmic problems.

Recognition asks for the actual membership bit on every graph. Property testing changes the required distinction by allowing graphs close to the property to have unconstrained answers. Goldreich’s discussion emphasizes this difference: constant-query proximity testers do not contradict a quadratic lower bound for recognition.

The saved manuscript only briefly describes randomized recognition. This card explicitly adopts the bounded-error convention already used in its working summary, corroborated by Buhrman and de Wolf’s Open Problem 6 and Grossman, Komargodski and Naor’s Conjecture 3.14. The no-error expected-cost question is a distinct weaker variant and is preserved as context, not silently conflated with this target.

For zero-error computation, every sampled deterministic tree is correct on every input and complexity is the largest, over inputs, expected query count. Chakrabarti and Khot prove \(\Omega(n^{4/3}(\log n)^{1/3})\) in that model. Their definition is narrower than algorithms allowed to give a wrong answer. The cited theorem is therefore not itself a proof of the same bound for this card’s larger algorithm class.

The deterministic Aanderaa–Karp–Rosenberg conjecture asks for the exact value \(\binom n2\) for every property at every size. Here the target allows a fixed multiplicative saving and concerns randomized algorithms. A quadratic randomized lower bound would not automatically establish the exact deterministic value. A quadratic deterministic lower bound alone does not exclude randomized savings.

The quantum analogue has a different scale. The 2020 result proves a universal \(\Omega(n)\) quantum-query lower bound, and the property of having at least one edge admits \(O(n)\) quantum queries. Resolving that linear-scale analogue does not resolve the quadratic classical randomized conjecture.
